bc_slhanay.blurb: Slhanay is the big granite dome just north of the Stawamus Chief, and its steep west-facing walls are reached from the Mamquam forest road rather than from the Chief's trails. The climbing is mostly multi-pitch trad on cracks and faces, with a few sport and aid lines mixed in. Grades cluster in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a handful of 5.12s, so it suits parties comfortable on sustained climbing. Tall walls and tree cover keep it shaded, which makes it a sensible summer choice when the Chief is baking.

bc_f_viper.blurb: Viper is one of the sectors of the Grand Wall Boulders, a maze of granite blocks scattered through mossy forest beneath the Stawamus Chief. Problems here run from VB up to V7, but most sit between V0 and V4, with the standout line, Viper (V5), giving the area its name. Slopers and compression moves are the theme. The forest keeps everything cool and shady, so summer sessions work well. Landings are often rocky or rooted, so bring a few small pads to fill gaps, and expect the trail network between blocks to be confusing on a first visit.
bc_f_viper.parking_note: Use the main Stawamus Chief lot off Highway 99 south of downtown Squamish, then walk toward the campground on the wide gravel track.
bc_f_viper.approach: Follow the gravel track past the campground; Black Dyke trail is the first path off Psych Ledge and leads into the Viper and Black Dyke blocks.

bc_top_shelf.blurb: Top Shelf is a steep granite wall above the Mamquam forest road, built around crack climbing. Nearly everything is trad, and the grades start around 5.10 and run past 5.13, with the bulk of routes in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, so there are few easy warm-ups. The rock is clean and solid and the wall is steeper than it looks, which makes for pumpy finger and hand cracks. Eye Catcher, an obvious left-facing dihedral, marks the base, and Cursed Crack is a short, technical finger line. Shade holds for most of the day. Bring doubles of cams from fingers to hands.
bc_top_shelf.parking_note: Pull off about 2.7 km up the Mamquam forest road; the trail starts on the right between the third and fourth pullouts.
bc_top_shelf.approach: Steep but well-worn forest trail. Keep left at the first cairned fork and right at the second, just before a mossy cliff; Eye Catcher is the landmark at the base.

bc_forgotten_wall.blurb: Forgotten Wall is a sport wall at the Chek crag in Cheakamus Canyon, tucked along one edge of the upper parking area. The rock is mostly overhanging, with routes up to about 25 m, and the grades lean hard: the majority sit at 5.11 and 5.12, a few go to 5.13, and there are only a handful of 5.10s and one 5.9. Creepy Crawlers and The Incredible Journey are among the best-known lines. Because the wall is so close to the car, it is quick to get on and easy to combine with neighbouring Chek walls.
bc_forgotten_wall.parking_note: Drive about 25 km north of Squamish on Highway 99 and turn right onto the Conroy Creek forest road, then follow the steep gravel up to the large upper lot.
bc_forgotten_wall.approach: The wall sits along the west edge of the upper lot; short paths through the trees reach its base.

bc_the_east_wall.blurb: The East Wall is the tallest face at Harrison Bluffs, an east-facing granite wall that holds three- and four-pitch climbs. The rock is edgier than elsewhere in the bluffs, so strong fingers help. Climbs are a mix of trad and bolted lines from about 5.6 to 5.11, with the largest cluster at 5.10. Jane's Journey and Pocket Crack are good examples of the moderates on offer. Low elevation keeps the bluffs climbable on sunny days well outside summer, and weekdays tend to be quiet. Spring brings heavy mosquitoes.
bc_the_east_wall.parking_note: From Agassiz take Harrison Hot Springs Road to the end of the golf course, turn through the yellow gate onto gravel, and park beside the electric tower after the small bridge.
bc_the_east_wall.approach: Take the trail east along the base of the bluffs toward the East Boulders, then climb uphill to the foot of the wall.

bc_east_boulders.blurb: The East Boulders are a scatter of granite blocks in the forest below the East Wall at Harrison Bluffs. Problems range from V0 to V9 and the middle grades, around V3 to V6, are best represented. Some blocks sit on the flat ground at the base of the cliff, where landings are decent but can be wet, while others are on the sloping hillside, where landings vary from flat to steep. The bluffs offer grippy, fine-grained granite, morning-to-midday sun and a long season from spring through autumn. Mosquitoes can be fierce in spring.
bc_east_boulders.approach: Walk east beneath the bluffs, passing the Kindergarten Wall; if the path disappears, drift out from the rock until you pick it up, and the first blocks come a minute or two later.

bc_ravens_wall.blurb: Ravens Wall is part of the Waterline Walls on the edge of Castlegar, a short walk from town. The face is steep and often overhanging, with roofs, prows and a left-facing corner, and the climbing is mostly bolted, powerful and sustained. Grades run from about 5.7 to 5.12, but the weight sits at 5.10 and above, with a good number of 5.12s. Lieutenant, Super Grover and Feather Quest are the lines most people come for.
bc_ravens_wall.parking_note: Drive west from Castlegar to the end of 14th Avenue and park where the dirt road ends.

bc_west_boulders.blurb: The West Boulders are one of two boulder zones at Harrison Bluffs, a granite crag between Agassiz and Harrison Hot Springs. The problems span the full range from VB through V9, with a notable number at the harder end of the scale. Granite here is fine-grained and grippy, with pockets formed by weathering. Sun arrives in the morning and runs to midday, and the low elevation makes sunny winter days usable, with the main season running spring through autumn. Spring mosquitoes can be bad. Weekdays are generally quiet.

bc_north_apron.blurb: North Apron is the steepest part of the Apron on the Stawamus Chief, split by many cracks and home to several classic moderates. The climbing is almost all multi-pitch trad on granite corners, cracks and slab, with a few sport lines. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, but the 5.9 to 5.11 range holds most routes. Rock On, St. Vitus' Dance and Calculus Crack are the sort of crack lines that draw crowds, so expect other parties on summer weekends. Carry a full trad rack and allow time for the descent.
bc_north_apron.approach: From the Apron lot, walk a short way up the Mamquam forest road, then take the climbers' trails into the trees on the right to the base near Calculus Crack.

bc_aberdeen_wall.blurb: Aberdeen Wall is one of the two main walls at the Aberdeen Columns, a plateau of columnar basalt in the hills above Vernon. The rock splits into tidy crack lines from about 12 to 25 m high, and nearly all of it is trad. Most routes fall between 5.9 and 5.11, with the 5.10s the most common and a few 5.12s. Karma Crack, Stem Cell and Ten-Digit Dialing are among the best. Cam placements are good, popular routes are clean, and the less-travelled ones may be mossy. The crag sits at altitude, so it runs cooler than the valley.
bc_aberdeen_wall.parking_note: Take the Goat Creek forest road to roughly 18 km and park just past the sharp bend.
bc_aberdeen_wall.approach: A signed trail leaves the east side of the road into the trees and passes under a large tree before the wall appears above. Watch for nettles.
